quotes.text: You will rarely see a comparable level of sheer musicianship on a live album. I almost typed "virtuosity", but then decided it was the wrong word. Not that Pete Townshend, John Entwistle, and Keith Moon weren't virtuosos on their respective instruments, there is really no question on that point, they clearly were. But virtuosity implies a technical proficiency that is actually far more common than musical creativity. With sufficient practice, most reasonably talented musicians can probably reach some level of virtuosity. But musical creativity – that is a far rarer gift indeed. These guys weren't just proficient – they were creative.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: The Who had a reputation for being loud, but they were also marvelously inventive. Just listen to that rhythm guitar – that kind of attack was unthinkable in rock only a few years prior, Townshend knew how to power a song along. He was an underrated rhythm guitarist for sure, besides being an excellent soloist.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: In the early 70s, he was that rare combination of guitar virtuoso and exceptional songwriter, although as the decade wore on he tended to display more of the former and less of the latter.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: I need to point out how important his sense of dynamics was to the sound of The Who – perhaps moreso than any guitarist that preceded him, he understood the importance of playing with a range of intensity. Despite their reputation as a loud band, Townshend was actually a pioneer in shifting up and down the decibel range.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: Listen to his performance here – surely he plays absolutely ferociously at times, but tempers it with quieter moments. Tommy was always full of those kinds of dynamic contrasts. I am convinced that two and half hours of a guitar, bass, and drums playing at full volume would get old before long, I think part of the key to Live at Leeds' success was the dynamic range of the playing, particularly Pete's.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: Jimmy Page would pretty much trademark the phrase "Light and Shade", but Townshend realized its importance before the Mighty Zep took flight.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: In a time when bass guitar was just coming into its own as an instrument that did more than merely hold down the bottom, John Entwistle was one of a handful of early bass guitar geniuses.
quotes.publication: The Who – Live at Leeds (Deluxe Edition)

quotes.text: This is a group that contributed to the framework of how rock 'n' roll musicians behave: They break instruments and have bad attitudes. They brand themselves: Who wouldn't readily identify that Union Jack target logo with the group? They make money: T-shirts on the current tour are fetching $40 a pop. They come up with signature moves (Townshend's jumping windmill guitar stroke) and they bare their chests (Daltrey).
The band's recordings are the heart of the matter, though, and go a long way toward reopening the case on the brilliant band.
Townshend's grandiose ideas were, as with Tommy and Quadrophenia, based in human struggle and funneled into operatic structure.
The playing is expectedly tired without Moon and Entwistle as anchors, yet it doesn't feel like a grown-up transition that, say, Robert Plant has made in recent years.
Here, the Who is playing to the newly established MTV market and it works, sparingly.
Together, Entwistle and Moon hold the rhythm section firm, but it's an odd effort.
